findings.title: CAROL@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL has GenericAll on CHILD_DA@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL
findings.summary: CAROL@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL is outside Tier Zero but has GenericAll on Tier Zero object CHILD_DA@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL (Member of DOMAIN ADMINS@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL). Whoever controls CAROL@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL controls CHILD_DA@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL.
findings.remediation: Remove the GenericAll permission that CAROL@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL holds on CHILD_DA@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL. It is inherited, so remove it where it is defined (on TIER0 ADMINS@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL or a container above it); that also removes it from every other object below that container.

findings.title: Kerberoastable account SVC_SQL@CONTOSO.LOCAL has a path to Tier Zero
findings.summary: SVC_SQL@CONTOSO.LOCAL has a service principal name, so any domain user can request a ticket encrypted with its password and crack it offline, and it has a path to Tier Zero. Its password was last set 6126 days ago.
findings.remediation: Remove unneeded SPNs from SVC_SQL@CONTOSO.LOCAL, or move the service to a group Managed Service Account (gMSA). If the SPN must stay, set a random password of 25+ characters and allow only AES Kerberos encryption for the account.

findings.title: SVC_SYNC@CONTOSO.LOCAL can DCSync CONTOSO.LOCAL
findings.summary: SVC_SYNC@CONTOSO.LOCAL holds both directory replication rights on CONTOSO.LOCAL. It can request the password hash of any account, including krbtgt, which is full domain compromise.
findings.remediation: Remove the 'Replicating Directory Changes' and 'Replicating Directory Changes All' rights granted to SVC_SYNC@CONTOSO.LOCAL on CONTOSO.LOCAL, or remove SVC_SYNC@CONTOSO.LOCAL from the group that grants them. Only domain controllers need these rights. If this is an Entra Connect or similar sync account, keep the rights but manage the account and its server as Tier Zero (`--tier-zero`).

findings.title: DA_ALICE@CONTOSO.LOCAL is logged on to 1 non-Tier Zero host(s)
findings.summary: Tier Zero account DA_ALICE@CONTOSO.LOCAL had sessions on SRV01.CONTOSO.LOCAL. Anyone with admin rights on those hosts can take its credentials from memory.
findings.remediation: Use a separate admin account per tier so DA_ALICE@CONTOSO.LOCAL only logs on to Tier Zero systems. Enforce it with 'Deny log on' user rights or Authentication Policy Silos, add the account to Protected Users, and log off or reboot the listed hosts to clear cached credentials.

findings.title: APP01.CONTOSO.LOCAL has unconstrained delegation
findings.summary: APP01.CONTOSO.LOCAL is trusted for unconstrained delegation. An attacker who controls it can coerce a domain controller to authenticate to it (PrinterBug, PetitPotam) and capture the DC's Kerberos ticket, so it is effectively Tier Zero.
findings.remediation: Disable unconstrained delegation on APP01.CONTOSO.LOCAL. Use constrained or resource-based constrained delegation for the specific services that need it. Until then, manage APP01.CONTOSO.LOCAL as Tier Zero and disable the Print Spooler on domain controllers to reduce coercion.

findings.title: Trust CONTOSO.LOCAL -> FABRIKAM.COM has SID filtering disabled
findings.summary: The External trust between CONTOSO.LOCAL and FABRIKAM.COM does not filter SIDs. An attacker who compromises the trusted side can forge SID history to gain privileged access across the trust.
findings.remediation: Enable SID filtering (quarantine) on the external trust: `netdom trust CONTOSO.LOCAL /domain:FABRIKAM.COM /quarantine:yes`. If a migration still needs SID history, plan when it ends and turn it off then.

findings.title: BOB@CONTOSO.LOCAL can log on to 1 domain controller(s) in CONTOSO.LOCAL (Remote Desktop)
findings.summary: BOB@CONTOSO.LOCAL is outside Tier Zero but can open a session on domain controllers through Remote Desktop: DC01.CONTOSO.LOCAL. A session on a DC is one local privilege escalation away from the whole domain, and it exposes the DC to whatever runs in that account's session.
findings.remediation: Remove BOB@CONTOSO.LOCAL from the built-in Remote Desktop Users (S-1-5-32-555) group of CONTOSO.LOCAL. On domain controllers these are domain groups shared by every DC, not local groups. Also check GPOs linked to the Domain Controllers OU for user rights that grant the same logon (for example 'Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services'). Administer DCs from Tier Zero accounts only.

findings.title: BOB@CONTOSO.LOCAL does not require Kerberos pre-authentication
findings.summary: Anyone on the network can request authentication data for BOB@CONTOSO.LOCAL that is encrypted with its password, without credentials, and crack it offline.
findings.remediation: Clear 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' on BOB@CONTOSO.LOCAL. If an application genuinely needs it, give the account a long random password.

findings.title: 1 Tier Zero account(s) in CONTOSO.LOCAL can be delegated
findings.summary: 1 Tier Zero account is neither in Protected Users nor marked 'sensitive and cannot be delegated', so its credentials can be cached on other systems or delegated to them.
findings.remediation: Add Tier Zero user accounts to the Protected Users group (test service accounts first), or at minimum set 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated'.

findings.title: 2 Tier Zero account(s) in CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL can be delegated
findings.summary: 2 Tier Zero accounts are neither in Protected Users nor marked 'sensitive and cannot be delegated', so their credentials can be cached on other systems or delegated to them.
findings.remediation: Add Tier Zero user accounts to the Protected Users group (test service accounts first), or at minimum set 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated'.

findings.title: 1 stale Tier Zero account(s) in CONTOSO.LOCAL
findings.summary: 1 enabled Tier Zero account has not logged on in over 90 days, or never. Unused privileged accounts are attack surface nobody is watching.
findings.remediation: Disable these accounts, or remove them from privileged groups if they are still needed.

findings.title: 1 Tier Zero password(s) older than 365 days in CONTOSO.LOCAL
findings.summary: 1 Tier Zero account has a password older than 365 days. Old passwords are more likely to have been exposed in past breaches, backups or memory dumps.
findings.remediation: Rotate these passwords. For service accounts, migrate to gMSAs so rotation is automatic.

findings.title: 2 computer(s) in CONTOSO.LOCAL without LAPS
findings.summary: 2 computers have local administrator passwords that LAPS doesn't manage. Unmanaged local admin passwords are often the same across machines, so one compromise spreads to the others.
findings.remediation: Deploy Windows LAPS to these computers and restrict who can read the stored passwords.

findings.title: KRBTGT@CONTOSO.LOCAL password is 6126 days old
findings.summary: The krbtgt key signs every Kerberos ticket in the domain. It was last changed 6126 days ago, so a golden ticket forged with a key stolen at any time since then still works.
findings.remediation: Rotate the krbtgt password twice, waiting at least the maximum ticket lifetime (10 hours by default) between rotations, using Microsoft's New-KrbtgtKeys script. Repeat at least every 180 days.

findings.title: 1 account(s) in CONTOSO.LOCAL allow an empty password
findings.summary: 1 enabled account has PASSWD_NOTREQD set, so its password may be empty whatever the password policy says.
findings.remediation: Clear the PASSWD_NOTREQD flag (userAccountControl 0x20) and reset each password.

fixes.action: Stop DA_ALICE@CONTOSO.LOCAL from logging on to SRV01.CONTOSO.LOCAL, then log off or reboot SRV01.CONTOSO.LOCAL to clear its cached credentials.

Remove the GenericAll permission that CAROL@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL holds on CHILD_DA@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL. It is inherited, so remove it where it is defined (on TIER0 ADMINS@CHILD.CONTOSO.LOCAL or a container above it); that also removes it from every other object below that container.

Remove the 'Replicating Directory Changes' and 'Replicating Directory Changes All' rights granted to SVC_SYNC@CONTOSO.LOCAL on CONTOSO.LOCAL, or remove SVC_SYNC@CONTOSO.LOCAL from the group that grants them.

guides.PW-002:
# PW-002: Non-Tier Zero principal can DCSync

**Category:** Attack path
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team

## What this finding means
A user, computer or group outside Tier Zero holds both directory replication
rights on the domain object: "Replicating Directory Changes" and "Replicating
Directory Changes All" (directly or through group membership). Together they let
it ask a domain controller for the password hash of any account.

## Why attackers care
DCSync (OS Credential Dumping: DCSync, T1003.006) lets an attacker who controls
this principal pull the krbtgt hash and every admin hash remotely, without touching
a domain controller's disk. With the krbtgt hash they can forge golden tickets and
keep domain access until krbtgt is rotated twice. Tools such as Mimikatz and
Impacket secretsdump do this in one command.

## Before you change anything
- Identify what the principal is. Legitimate holders besides domain controllers
  are rare: Entra Connect (MSOL_ / AAD sync) accounts, some identity governance,
  backup or password-sync products.
- Check whether it actually replicates: on domain controllers, audit
  "Directory Service Access" and look for event 4662 with the replication GUIDs
  `1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2` and `1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2`
  and the principal as subject.
- If it is a sync account that must keep the rights, do not remove them: treat the
  account and its server as Tier Zero instead (Option B).

## Fix
### Option A: Remove the replication rights (recommended when not needed)
1. In **Active Directory Users and Computers**, enable **View > Advanced Features**.
2. Right-click the domain, **Properties > Security > Advanced**.
3. Find entries for the principal (or the group that grants it) with
   "Replicating Directory Changes" / "Replicating Directory Changes All".
4. Select each and click **Remove**, then **OK**.
5. If the right comes through a group, remove the principal from that group instead.
### Option B: Keep the rights, manage the principal as Tier Zero
1. Add the account and the server it runs on to `tier_zero` in `pathwarden.toml`.
2. Restrict logon to that server to Tier Zero admins, protect the account
   (long random password or gMSA where the product supports it), and monitor
   event 4662 for replication from any other source.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory
$domainDN = (Get-ADDomain).DistinguishedName
$acl = Get-Acl -Path "AD:\$domainDN"

# Replication extended rights
$getChanges    = [Guid]"1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2"
$getChangesAll = [Guid]"1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2"

# Show who holds them
$acl.Access | Where-Object { $_.ObjectType -in $getChanges, $getChangesAll } |
    Select-Object IdentityReference, ObjectType, IsInherited

# Save the current descriptor, then remove the principal's entries
$acl.Sddl | Out-File ".\domain-acl-backup.txt"
$acl.Access | Where-Object {
    $_.ObjectType -in $getChanges, $getChangesAll -and $_.IdentityReference -like "*<Account>"
} | ForEach-Object { [void]$acl.RemoveAccessRule($_) }
Set-Acl -Path "AD:\$domainDN" -AclObject $acl
```

## Verify
Re-run the "Show who holds them" query; only domain controllers, Enterprise Domain
Controllers, Administrators and intended sync accounts should remain. Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

## Rollback
Restore the saved descriptor:
`$acl = Get-Acl "AD:\$domainDN"; $acl.SetSecurityDescriptorSddlForm((Get-Content .\domain-acl-backup.txt)); Set-Acl "AD:\$domainDN" $acl`

## References
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/006/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-configure-ad-ds-connector-account
- https://bloodhound.specterops.io/
guides.PW-003:
# PW-003: Non-Tier Zero principal controls a Tier Zero object

**Category:** Attack path
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team (server team for local rights, PKI team for ManageCA)

## What this finding means
A principal outside Tier Zero holds a permission or relationship over a Tier Zero
object (a privileged account or group, a domain controller, a Tier Zero GPO or OU,
a certificate authority). Whoever controls that principal can take over the Tier
Zero object, so Tier Zero is only as safe as the weaker principal.

## Why attackers care
Attackers chain these relationships: compromise a helpdesk account, use its
GenericAll on a Domain Admin to reset the password (T1098, Account Manipulation),
or its local admin rights on a server where an admin is logged on. Each edge kind
has a known, tool-supported abuse; BloodHound shows them all in one graph.

## Before you change anything
- Check whether the permission is inherited: the finding names the container to
  fix if so. Removing it there also removes it from every object below.
- Find out who uses it: Directory Service Changes auditing (event 5136) on the
  target shows modifications; for local rights check logon events 4624 on the host.
- Back up the security descriptor before editing:
  `(Get-Acl "AD:\<TargetDN>").Sddl | Out-File .\acl-backup.txt`

## Fix
### Option A: Remove the relationship (recommended)
Use the table for the edge in the finding.

| Edge | Fix |
|---|---|
| GenericAll, GenericWrite, WriteDacl, WriteOwner, AllExtendedRights, AddMember, AddSelf, ForceChangePassword, AddKeyCredentialLink, AddAllowedToAct, WriteSPN, WriteAccountRestrictions, WriteGPLink, ReadLAPSPassword, ReadGMSAPassword, SyncLAPSPassword | ADUC (Advanced Features) > target **Properties > Security > Advanced** > remove the entry (on the parent if inherited) |
| Owns | Same dialog > **Owner: Change** to Domain Admins |
| GPLink | GPMC: restrict who can edit the GPO, or unlink it from the Tier Zero OU |
| AdminTo, CanRDP, ExecuteDCOM, CanPSRemote | Remove the principal from the local group on the host or from the GPO that adds it |
| AllowedToDelegate | Target **Properties > Delegation**: remove the Tier Zero service from the list |
| AllowedToAct | Clear the principal from `msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity` |
| HasSIDHistory | Clear `sIDHistory` on the principal |
| ManageCA | certsrv.msc > CA **Properties > Security** > remove Manage CA |

### Option B: Move the principal into Tier Zero
If the principal genuinely administers Tier Zero, add it to `tier_zero` in
`pathwarden.toml` and protect it like Tier Zero (dedicated admin account, Tier Zero
logon restrictions). Use this only for real Tier Zero administrators.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory
$dn  = (Get-ADObject -Identity "<TargetDN>").DistinguishedName
$acl = Get-Acl -Path "AD:\$dn"

# Show the principal's entries
$acl.Access | Where-Object { $_.IdentityReference -like "*<Principal>" } |
    Select-Object ActiveDirectoryRights, ObjectType, IsInherited

# Remove explicit entries for the principal
$acl.Access | Where-Object { $_.IdentityReference -like "*<Principal>" -and -not $_.IsInherited } |
    ForEach-Object { [void]$acl.RemoveAccessRule($_) }
Set-Acl -Path "AD:\$dn" -AclObject $acl

# Owns: hand ownership back to Domain Admins
$acl = Get-Acl -Path "AD:\$dn"
$acl.SetOwner([System.Security.Principal.NTAccount]"<Domain>\Domain Admins")
Set-Acl -Path "AD:\$dn" -AclObject $acl

# HasSIDHistory: clear SID history
Set-ADUser -Identity "<Principal>" -Clear sIDHistory

# AllowedToAct: clear resource-based constrained delegation on the target computer
Set-ADComputer -Identity "<Computer>" -PrincipalsAllowedToDelegateToAccount $null
```

## Verify
Re-run the "Show the principal's entries" query on the target (and on the parent if
inherited); it should return nothing. Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

## Rollback
Restore the saved descriptor:
`$acl = Get-Acl "AD:\$dn"; $acl.SetSecurityDescriptorSddlForm((Get-Content .\acl-backup.txt)); Set-Acl "AD:\$dn" $acl`.
For local group or delegation changes, re-add the removed entry.

## References
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/
- https://bloodhound.specterops.io/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/plan/security-best-practices/best-practices-for-securing-active-directory
guides.PW-004:
# PW-004: Tier Zero account logged on to non-Tier Zero hosts

**Category:** Attack path
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team together with the admins who own the account

## What this finding means
A Tier Zero account (for example a Domain Admin) had a session on servers or
workstations outside Tier Zero. While logged on, and often afterwards, its
credentials are in that host's memory, so anyone with admin rights on the host can
take them.

## Why attackers care
Attackers who gain local admin on any listed host dump LSASS or steal Kerberos
tickets (OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory, T1003.001) and immediately become
Domain Admin. This is one of the most common paths in real intrusions and pentests,
and usually the biggest choke point in `pathwarden plan`.

## Before you change anything
- Ask the account owner why they log on to those hosts (RDP, scheduled task,
  service, mapped drive). Event 4624 on the host shows logon type: 2/10 interactive
  or RDP, 3 network, 4 batch, 5 service.
- Services or scheduled tasks running as a Tier Zero account must be moved to a
  dedicated, non-privileged service account (or gMSA) first, or they will break.
- Make sure each admin has a separate, non-Tier Zero account for daily work.

## Fix
### Option A: Separate accounts per tier and deny Tier Zero logon elsewhere (recommended)
1. Give the admin a normal account for workstations and a Tier 1 account for
   servers if needed.
2. In **Group Policy Management**, edit a GPO linked to all non-Tier Zero
   computers: **Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security
   Settings > Local Policies > User Rights Assignment**.
3. Add the Tier Zero groups (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins) to
   **Deny log on locally**, **Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services**,
   **Deny log on as a batch job** and **Deny log on as a service**.
4. Log off the account on the listed hosts, or reboot them, to clear cached
   credentials.
### Option B: Authentication Policy Silos
1. In **Active Directory Administrative Center > Authentication**, create an
   authentication policy and silo that allows Tier Zero accounts to authenticate
   only from Tier Zero hosts (requires Windows Server 2012 R2+ domain functional level).
2. Assign the accounts and Tier Zero hosts to the silo; test in audit mode first.
### Option C: Protected Users
Add the account to **Protected Users**: no NTLM, no delegation, no cached
credentials, 4-hour TGTs. Test first: it breaks NTLM-only apps for that account.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Where has the account logged on recently? (run on a host from the finding)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName = 'Security'; Id = 4624 } -MaxEvents 2000 |
    Where-Object { $_.Properties[5].Value -eq '<Account>' } |
    Select-Object TimeCreated, @{ n = 'LogonType'; e = { $_.Properties[8].Value } }

# Services and scheduled tasks running as the account on a host
Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -ComputerName <Computer> | Where-Object StartName -like '*<Account>*'
Get-ScheduledTask -CimSession <Computer> | Where-Object { $_.Principal.UserId -like '*<Account>*' }

# Add the account to Protected Users (after testing)
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Protected Users" -Members "<Account>"
```

## Verify
After the deny rights apply (`gpupdate /force`, or the next refresh), a logon attempt
by the Tier Zero account on a listed host must fail. Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

## Rollback
Remove the groups from the Deny user rights in the GPO (or unlink it) and run
`gpupdate /force`; remove the account from Protected Users with
`Remove-ADGroupMember "Protected Users" -Members "<Account>"`.

## References
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/credentials-protection-and-management/protected-users-security-group
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/credentials-protection-and-management/authentication-policies-and-authentication-policy-silos
guides.PW-005:
# PW-005: Unconstrained delegation outside domain controllers

**Category:** Attack path
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team with the server or application owner

## What this finding means
A computer or user that is not a domain controller is "trusted for delegation to
any service" (unconstrained delegation). Every account that authenticates to it
with Kerberos leaves a forwardable ticket (TGT) in its memory. That makes the host
as sensitive as a domain controller.

## Why attackers care
An attacker with admin rights on the host coerces a domain controller to
authenticate to it (PrinterBug / MS-RPRN, PetitPotam / MS-EFSR), captures the DC's
TGT from memory and uses it to DCSync the domain (Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets,
T1558). No credentials of the victim DC are needed; only control of this host.

## Before you change anything
- Ask the application owner why delegation was enabled. Common legacy reasons: IIS
  or SQL Server front ends that access back-end services as the user.
- Identify which back-end services the host must delegate to (SPNs). Kerberos
  service ticket events 4769 on domain controllers with this host as the requesting
  service show what it actually requests.
- Constrained or resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) supports nearly all
  such scenarios; plan the replacement before removing the flag.

## Fix
### Option A: Switch to constrained delegation (recommended)
1. **Active Directory Users and Computers** > the computer (or service account) >
   **Properties > Delegation**.
2. Select **Trust this computer for delegation to specified services only**, then
   **Use Kerberos only** where possible.
3. **Add** only the back-end services (SPNs) the application needs, **OK**.
### Option B: Remove delegation entirely
If nothing needs it, select **Do not trust this computer for delegation**.
### Option C: Resource-based constrained delegation
Configure delegation on the back-end resource instead (its
`PrincipalsAllowedToDelegateToAccount`), which keeps control with the resource owner.

Until fixed, manage the host as Tier Zero, and disable the Print Spooler service on
domain controllers to reduce coercion.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Find all non-DC principals with unconstrained delegation
Get-ADComputer -Filter { TrustedForDelegation -eq $true -and PrimaryGroupID -ne 516 -and PrimaryGroupID -ne 521 } -Properties TrustedForDelegation
Get-ADUser -Filter { TrustedForDelegation -eq $true } -Properties TrustedForDelegation

# Remove unconstrained delegation from one computer
Set-ADAccountControl -Identity "<Computer>$" -TrustedForDelegation $false

# Optional: constrained delegation to a specific back-end service
Set-ADComputer -Identity "<Computer>" -Add @{ 'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo' = 'MSSQLSvc/<backend>.<domain>:1433' }

# Resource-based alternative, set on the back-end computer
Set-ADComputer -Identity "<BackendComputer>" -PrincipalsAllowedToDelegateToAccount (Get-ADComputer "<Computer>")
```

## Verify
`Get-ADComputer "<Computer>" -Properties TrustedForDelegation` must show `False`.
Test the application end to end as a normal user. Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

## Rollback
`Set-ADAccountControl -Identity "<Computer>$" -TrustedForDelegation $true` restores
the previous setting. Clear any added constrained delegation with
`Set-ADComputer "<Computer>" -Clear msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo`.

## References
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/kerberos/kerberos-constrained-delegation-overview
guides.PW-006:
# PW-006: Kerberoastable account with Tier Zero access

**Category:** Attack path
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team with the service owner

## What this finding means
A user account with a service principal name (SPN) is in Tier Zero or has a path
to it. Any domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket for it, and that
ticket is encrypted with a key derived from the account's password.

## Why attackers care
Kerberoasting (Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting, T1558.003) needs only
a normal domain account: request tickets for every SPN, take them offline and crack
the passwords. Service account passwords are often old, human-chosen and never
rotated, and RC4 tickets crack quickly. A cracked privileged service account means
domain compromise without any alert on the target.

## Before you change anything
- Identify the service using the SPN (`setspn -L <Account>`), the hosts running it,
  and who owns it.
- Check whether the SPN is still used: event 4769 on domain controllers shows
  service ticket requests for the account. No requests over weeks often means a
  stale SPN.
- If the account is privileged only because of a group it does not need (common
  for old SQL service accounts in Domain Admins), removing that membership is part
  of the fix.

## Fix
### Option A: Move the service to a group Managed Service Account (recommended)
1. Create a gMSA (`New-ADServiceAccount`) allowed for the service's hosts.
2. Install it on the hosts (`Install-ADServiceAccount`) and change the service to
   run as `<Domain>\<gMSA>$` with an empty password.
3. Move the SPNs to the gMSA, then disable the old account.
gMSA passwords are 120 random characters rotated automatically: not crackable.
### Option B: Remove unneeded SPNs or privileges
Remove stale SPNs with `setspn -D`, and remove the account from privileged groups it
does not need.
### Option C: If the account must stay
Set a random password of 25+ characters, enable AES-only Kerberos for the account
("This account supports Kerberos AES 128/256 bit encryption" in ADUC **Account**
tab), and rotate the password on a schedule.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Kerberoastable user accounts
Get-ADUser -Filter { ServicePrincipalName -like "*" } -Properties ServicePrincipalName, PasswordLastSet, MemberOf

# Option A: create a gMSA (needs a KDS root key in the forest)
New-ADServiceAccount -Name "<gMSA>" -DNSHostName "<gMSA>.<Domain>" `
    -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword "<ServerGroup>"
Install-ADServiceAccount -Identity "<gMSA>"     # run on each service host

# Option B: remove a stale SPN
setspn -D <SPN> <Account>

# Option C: AES only (0x18 = AES128 + AES256), then reset the password
Set-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Replace @{ 'msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes' = 24 }
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity "<Account>" -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString "New password")
```

## Verify
`Get-ADUser "<Account>" -Properties ServicePrincipalName` shows no SPNs (Options A/B),
or `msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes` is 24 and PasswordLastSet is recent (Option C).
Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

## Rollback
Re-register an SPN with `setspn -S <SPN> <Account>`; switch the service back to the
old account in the Services console. Keep the old account disabled, not deleted,
until the gMSA has run cleanly for a while.

## References
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/003/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/group-managed-service-accounts/group-managed-service-accounts-overview
guides.PW-007:
# PW-007: Kerberos pre-authentication disabled (AS-REP roasting)

**Category:** Attack path or hygiene (hygiene when the account has no path to Tier Zero)
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team

## What this finding means
The account has "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication" set. Anyone who can
reach a domain controller can request an authentication response for it without
knowing its password, and part of that response is encrypted with the password.

## Why attackers care
AS-REP roasting (Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting, T1558.004) does
not even need a domain account: an attacker on the network asks for the response and
cracks it offline. If the password is weak, they get the account; if the account is
privileged or has a path to Tier Zero, that is domain compromise.

## Before you change anything
- The flag is almost always a leftover from old Unix/Kerberos interop or a vendor
  install guide. Ask the account owner which system uses it.
- Check recent use: event 4768 on domain controllers with "Pre-Authentication Type"
  0 for this account shows clients authenticating without pre-auth.
- Very old MIT Kerberos or Java clients may fail once pre-auth is required; test with
  the owning application.

## Fix
### Option A: Require pre-authentication (recommended)
1. **Active Directory Users and Computers** > the account > **Properties > Account**.
2. Under **Account options**, clear **Do not require Kerberos preauthentication**.
3. **OK**, then test the application that uses the account.
### Option B: If an application genuinely needs it
Keep the flag only with a long random password (25+ characters), no privileged group
memberships, and monitoring of event 4768 for that account.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# All accounts with pre-authentication disabled
Get-ADUser -Filter { DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true } -Properties DoesNotRequirePreAuth, Enabled

# Require pre-authentication again
Set-ADAccountControl -Identity "<Account>" -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false

# Option B: set a long random password if the flag must stay
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity "<Account>" -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString "New password")
```

## Verify
`Get-ADUser "<Account>" -Properties DoesNotRequirePreAuth` must show `False`. Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

## Rollback
`Set-ADAccountControl -Identity "<Account>" -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $true` restores the
previous behavior if an application breaks; then plan Option B for that account.

## References
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/004/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/activedirectory/set-adaccountcontrol
guides.PW-008:
# PW-008: Tier Zero accounts without delegation protection

**Category:** Hygiene
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team

## What this finding means
These Tier Zero user accounts are neither members of the Protected Users group nor marked
"Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated". Their credentials can therefore be cached on the
machines they log on to, and their Kerberos tickets can be forwarded by any service trusted for
delegation.

## Why attackers care
An attacker who controls a server trusted for unconstrained or constrained delegation can
impersonate any delegatable account that authenticates to it, including Domain Admins
(Kerberos delegation abuse, MITRE ATT&CK T1558). Accounts outside Protected Users also leave
NTLM hashes and long-lived credentials in LSASS memory, which tools like Mimikatz extract
(OS Credential Dumping, T1003.001). Protected Users removes both of these options for its members.

## Before you change anything
- Protected Users members **cannot** use NTLM, DES or RC4 Kerberos encryption, Kerberos
  delegation, or cached (offline) logons, and their Kerberos TGTs last 4 hours. Anything
  that relies on these will break for the account.
- Never add service accounts or computer accounts to Protected Users. Use the
  "sensitive and cannot be delegated" flag (Option B) for service accounts that are Tier Zero.
- Check for NTLM use by the account first: enable NTLM auditing
  ("Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit NTLM authentication in this domain") and review
  event 8004 on domain controllers, or 4624 events with Authentication Package NTLM.
- Make sure the domain functional level is Windows Server 2012 R2 or later. Protected Users
  only takes full effect from that level.
- Keep at least one break-glass account **outside** Protected Users in case Kerberos fails.
  Store its password offline.

## Fix
### Option A: Add Tier Zero user accounts to Protected Users (recommended)
1. Open **Active Directory Users and Computers** (dsa.msc).
2. Go to the **Users** container and open the **Protected Users** group.
3. **Members** tab > **Add**. Add one test admin account first.
4. Sign out and sign back in with that account. Confirm your admin tools still work.
5. Add the remaining interactive Tier Zero admin accounts listed in the finding.

### Option B: Mark the account "sensitive and cannot be delegated"
Use this for accounts that cannot join Protected Users, such as Tier Zero service accounts.
1. In dsa.msc, open the account > **Account** tab.
2. Under **Account options**, tick **Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated**.
3. Click **OK**.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Option A: add an interactive admin account to Protected Users
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity "Protected Users" -Members "<Account>"

# Option B: block delegation for an account that cannot join Protected Users
Set-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -AccountNotDelegated $true
```

## Verify
```powershell
# Members of Protected Users
Get-ADGroupMember -Identity "Protected Users" | Select-Object SamAccountName

# Accounts flagged as not delegatable
Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties AccountNotDelegated |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, AccountNotDelegated
```
Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone (or lists fewer accounts).

## Rollback
- Remove the account from the group: `Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity "Protected Users" -Members "<Account>"`.
  The change applies at the account's next logon. Existing tickets expire within 4 hours.
- Clear the flag: `Set-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -AccountNotDelegated $false`.

## References
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/credentials-protection-and-management/protected-users-security-group
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
guides.PW-009:
# PW-009: Stale Tier Zero accounts

**Category:** Hygiene
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team

## What this finding means
These accounts are enabled and hold Tier Zero privileges, but they have not logged on within the
configured period (90 days by default) or have never logged on at all. Nobody appears to use them,
yet they could still take over the domain.

## Why attackers care
Dormant privileged accounts are ideal targets. Their passwords are often old or reused, and
nobody notices when they are used again. An attacker who guesses, sprays or cracks such a password
gets Tier Zero access through a legitimate account (Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts, MITRE
ATT&CK T1078.002). Unused accounts also tend to sit outside monitoring and MFA rollouts.

## Before you change anything
- Confirm with the account owner (from the description, the manager attribute or your IAM
  system) that the account is not needed.
- Service accounts may authenticate without updating lastLogonTimestamp the way you expect.
  Check for recent 4624 / 4768 / 4769 events for the account on domain controllers before disabling.
- lastLogonTimestamp replicates with up to a 14-day lag. Treat dates as approximate.
- For break-glass accounts that are meant to be unused, document them and suppress the finding
  in `pathwarden.toml` with an expiry date instead of disabling them.

## Fix
### Option A: Disable the account (recommended)
1. Open **Active Directory Users and Computers** (dsa.msc).
2. Find the account, right-click > **Disable Account**.
3. Add a note in the **Description** field (date, ticket number) and leave it disabled for a
   grace period (for example 30 days) before deleting it.

### Option B: Remove the privileged group memberships
If the account must stay enabled, for example for a rarely used process:
1. Open the account > **Member Of** tab.
2. Remove Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Administrators and any other Tier Zero group.
3. Grant only the specific rights the process needs.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Review last logon and group memberships first
Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties LastLogonDate, MemberOf, Description |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, LastLogonDate, Description, MemberOf

# Option A: disable and annotate
Disable-ADAccount -Identity "<Account>"
Set-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Description "Disabled <date> - stale Tier Zero account, ticket <ID>"

# Option B: remove from a privileged group instead
Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity "Domain Admins" -Members "<Account>" -Confirm:$false
```

## Verify
```powershell
Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties Enabled, MemberOf |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, Enabled, MemberOf
```
Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone (or lists fewer accounts).

## Rollback
- Re-enable the account with `Enable-ADAccount -Identity "<Account>"`.
- Re-add removed group memberships with `Add-ADGroupMember`. Record the original
  memberships (the review command above) before removing them.

## References
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/002/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/plan/security-best-practices/implementing-least-privilege-administrative-models
guides.PW-010:
# PW-010: Old Tier Zero passwords

**Category:** Hygiene
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team (service account owners for service accounts)

## What this finding means
These Tier Zero accounts have passwords older than the configured limit (365 days by default).
The longer a privileged password lives, the more places it may have leaked to: old backups,
scripts, memory dumps, password managers of former staff, or earlier breaches.

## Why attackers care
Attackers routinely recover old credential material, such as NTDS.dit backups, LSASS dumps from
decommissioned servers and cracked hashes from earlier intrusions. A password that has not changed
since then still works (Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts, MITRE ATT&CK T1078.002). If an attacker
has the NTLM hash of an unchanged account, pass-the-hash keeps working until the password changes
(Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash, T1550.002).

## Before you change anything
- For **service accounts**, find every place the password is configured (services, scheduled
  tasks, IIS application pools, application config files, scripts) before rotating. Check
  4625 failures on domain controllers right after the change to catch anything you missed.
- Check for "password never expires": `Get-ADUser <Account> -Properties PasswordNeverExpires`.
- Interactive admins should change their own password so they choose and store it securely.
- Prefer migrating service accounts to group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA), which rotate
  automatically.

## Fix
### Option A: Rotate the password now (recommended)
1. Open **Active Directory Users and Computers** (dsa.msc).
2. Right-click the account > **Reset Password**.
3. Set a long random password (25+ characters for service accounts) and store it in your
   privileged access vault.
4. For service accounts, update every place that uses the password, then restart the dependent
   services.

### Option B: Move service accounts to a gMSA
1. Create a gMSA (`New-ADServiceAccount`) that the hosts running the service are allowed to use.
2. Install it on those hosts (`Install-ADServiceAccount`) and reconfigure the service to run as
   `<Domain>\<gMSA>$` with an empty password.
3. Disable the old account once the service runs under the gMSA.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Review password age
Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties PasswordLastSet, PasswordNeverExpires |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, PasswordLastSet, PasswordNeverExpires

# Reset the password (prompts for the new value without echoing it)
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity "<Account>" -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString "New password")

# Optional: let the normal password policy apply again
Set-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -PasswordNeverExpires $false
```

## Verify
```powershell
Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties PasswordLastSet |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, PasswordLastSet
```
Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone (or lists fewer accounts).

## Rollback
A password cannot be "un-rotated". If a service breaks, set the new password wherever the
service is configured (or reset again to a value you control and update the service), then
restart the service. Check 4625 events to find the failing host.

## References
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/002/
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/group-managed-service-accounts/group-managed-service-accounts-overview
guides.PW-011:
# PW-011: Computers without LAPS

**Category:** Hygiene
**Typical owner:** Desktop / server team, with the AD team for schema and permissions

## What this finding means
These enabled computers (domain controllers excluded) do not have their local administrator
password managed by LAPS. Their built-in local Administrator password is probably set by an
image or a script, and is often identical across many machines.

## Why attackers care
After compromising one computer, an attacker dumps the local Administrator hash from the SAM and
tries it everywhere. If the password is shared, every computer with the same password falls
(Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash, MITRE ATT&CK T1550.002, and Lateral
Movement via SMB/Windows Admin Shares, T1021.002). This is one of the most common ways a single
phished workstation turns into domain-wide compromise during a pentest.

## Before you change anything
- Windows LAPS is built into Windows 10/11 and Windows Server 2019 and later with the April 2023
  update. Older systems need legacy Microsoft LAPS, or an upgrade.
- Decide who may read passwords. By default only Domain Admins can. Grant read access to a
  dedicated helpdesk/desktop group per OU, never to broad groups.
- Check for tooling that relies on the shared local admin password (deployment scripts, remote
  support tools) and move it to LAPS retrieval or domain accounts first.
- The schema update is forest-wide and needs Schema Admins rights. Plan it with the AD team.

## Fix
### Option A: Deploy Windows LAPS by Group Policy (recommended)
1. Extend the schema once: run `Update-LapsADSchema` as a Schema Admin.
2. Let computers write their own password: `Set-LapsADComputerSelfPermission -Identity "<OU>"`.
3. Grant read access to the support group: `Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission -Identity "<OU>" -AllowedPrincipals "<Domain>\<SupportGroup>"`.
4. In **Group Policy Management**, create a GPO linked to the OU and open
   **Computer Configuration > Policies > Administrative Templates > System > LAPS**.
5. Enable **Configure password backup directory** = **Active Directory**, and set
   **Password Settings** (complexity, length 15+, age 30 days).
6. Run `gpupdate /force` on a test computer and check that a password appears (see Verify).
7. Widen the GPO to the remaining OUs in the finding.

### Option B: Intune (for Entra-joined or co-managed devices)
Use an Intune **Endpoint security > Account protection > Local admin password solution**
policy with the backup directory set to Active Directory (for hybrid-joined) or Entra ID.

### PowerShell
```powershell
# One-time forest preparation (Schema Admins)
Update-LapsADSchema

# Per OU: allow computers to update their own password attributes
Set-LapsADComputerSelfPermission -Identity "<OU>"

# Per OU: allow the support group to read passwords
Set-LapsADReadPasswordPermission -Identity "<OU>" -AllowedPrincipals "<Domain>\<SupportGroup>"

# After GPO deployment: confirm a computer has a managed password
Get-LapsADPassword -Identity "<Computer>" -AsPlainText
```

## Verify
`Get-LapsADPassword -Identity "<Computer>"` returns a password and an expiration time. On the
client, the event log **Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > LAPS > Operational**
shows successful password updates. Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone (or lists
fewer computers).

## Rollback
Unlink or disable the LAPS GPO. Computers keep their last LAPS-set password, so retrieve it with
`Get-LapsADPassword` before removing read permissions. The schema extension is permanent but
harmless.

## References
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/laps/laps-overview
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/laps/laps-scenarios-windows-server-active-directory
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1550/002/
guides.PW-012:
# PW-012: Cross-forest trust without SID filtering

**Category:** Hygiene
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team

## What this finding means
This external or forest trust does not filter security identifiers (SIDs). Authentication
coming from the trusted domain may carry SIDs that belong to your domain, for example in the
SID history of an account, and your domain will honour them.

## Why attackers care
An attacker who compromises the trusted domain can forge a Kerberos ticket that includes the SID
of a privileged group in your domain, such as Domain Admins, in its SID history. Without
filtering, your domain grants that access across the trust (Access Token Manipulation: SID-History
Injection, MITRE ATT&CK T1134.005). The other forest's security then becomes yours: a breach there
is a breach here.

## Before you change anything
- SID filtering is usually disabled on purpose during a **migration**, so migrated accounts keep
  access through their old SIDs in sIDHistory. Confirm with the AD team whether a migration is
  still running.
- Find users who still depend on SID history: `Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties SIDHistory | Where-Object SIDHistory`.
  Re-permission their resources with their new SIDs before enabling filtering.
- Enabling quarantine on an **external** trust also filters SIDs from other domains in the
  trusted forest. Plan for access that crosses those domains.

## Fix
### Option A: Enable SID filtering (quarantine) on the trust (recommended)
Run on a domain controller of the trusting domain (the domain that grants access), as a
Domain Admin. `<TrustingDomain>` is the domain shown first in the finding title.
1. Open an elevated command prompt.
2. Run: `netdom trust <TrustingDomain> /domain:<TrustedDomain> /quarantine:yes`
3. For a **forest** trust, also make sure SID history is not enabled across it:
   `netdom trust <TrustingDomain> /domain:<TrustedDomain> /enablesidhistory:no`

### Option B: Finish the migration, clean up SID history, then filter
1. Re-permission resources that still rely on old SIDs.
2. Clear sIDHistory from migrated accounts.
3. Apply Option A.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Inspect the trust (SIDFilteringQuarantined / SIDFilteringForestAware columns)
Get-ADTrust -Filter "Target -eq '<TrustedDomain>'" |
    Select-Object Name, Direction, TrustType, SIDFilteringQuarantined, SIDFilteringForestAware

# Find accounts that still carry SID history
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties SIDHistory | Where-Object { $_.SIDHistory } |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, SIDHistory

# Enable quarantine (run from an elevated prompt on a DC of the trusting domain)
netdom trust <TrustingDomain> /domain:<TrustedDomain> /quarantine:yes
```

## Verify
`netdom trust <TrustingDomain> /domain:<TrustedDomain> /quarantine` reports that SID filtering is
enabled. Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

## Rollback
`netdom trust <TrustingDomain> /domain:<TrustedDomain> /quarantine:no` restores the previous
behaviour. Do this only temporarily, and with a dated suppression in `pathwarden.toml`.

## References
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1134/005/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/netdom-trust
guides.PW-013:
# PW-013: Accounts that may have an empty password

**Category:** Hygiene
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team

## What this finding means
These enabled accounts have the PASSWD_NOTREQD flag (userAccountControl 0x20) set. With this
flag, the account is exempt from the domain password policy and may have an empty password. The
flag is often left behind by old provisioning tools or scripted account creation.

## Why attackers care
Attackers enumerate accounts with this flag (any domain user can read userAccountControl) and try
a blank password against each one. A hit gives a working domain account with no cracking needed
(Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts, MITRE ATT&CK T1078.002). If any of these accounts is privileged,
the finding is rated higher because it is a direct route to Tier Zero.

## Before you change anything
- Find out which tool created the accounts. Some provisioning systems set the flag again on their
  next sync. Fix the tool's template as well.
- Clearing the flag does not change the current password. If the password is actually empty,
  the account keeps working with an empty password until you reset it.
- For service accounts, find where the password is configured before resetting it (see PW-010).

## Fix
### Option A: Clear the flag and reset the password (recommended)
1. Clear the flag with PowerShell (below). Active Directory Users and Computers does not show
   this flag; to do it in the GUI, use the **Attribute Editor** tab and remove 0x20 from
   **userAccountControl**.
2. In **Active Directory Users and Computers**, right-click the account > **Reset Password** and
   set a strong password.
3. For service accounts, update the password wherever it is configured and restart the services.

### Option B: Disable unused accounts
If an account in the list is not needed, disable it instead (`Disable-ADAccount`).

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# List enabled accounts with PASSWD_NOTREQD (0x20)
Get-ADUser -LDAPFilter "(&(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=32)(!(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=2)))" |
    Select-Object SamAccountName

# Clear the flag
Set-ADAccountControl -Identity "<Account>" -PasswordNotRequired $false

# Reset the password so it meets policy (prompts without echoing)
Set-ADAccountPassword -Identity "<Account>" -Reset -NewPassword (Read-Host -AsSecureString "New password")
```

## Verify
```powershell
Get-ADUser -Identity "<Account>" -Properties PasswordNotRequired |
    Select-Object SamAccountName, PasswordNotRequired
```
`PasswordNotRequired` should be `False`. Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone (or lists
fewer accounts).

## Rollback
`Set-ADAccountControl -Identity "<Account>" -PasswordNotRequired $true` restores the flag. This
is rarely needed: an account with a valid password works the same with or without the flag.

## References
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/active-directory/useraccountcontrol-manipulate-account-properties
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/002/
guides.PW-014:
# PW-014: krbtgt password not rotated

**Category:** Hygiene
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team

## What this finding means
The krbtgt account's password has not been changed within the configured period (180 days by
default). The key derived from this password signs and encrypts every Kerberos ticket-granting
ticket (TGT) in the domain.

## Why attackers care
Anyone who has ever obtained the krbtgt hash, for example through DCSync, a stolen DC backup or a
past breach, can forge TGTs for any user with any group membership. These are "golden tickets"
(Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket, MITRE ATT&CK T1558.001). The forged tickets keep
working until the krbtgt password has been changed **twice**, because domain controllers accept
both the current and the previous key. Regular rotation limits how long a stolen key stays useful.

## Before you change anything
- Make sure Active Directory replication is healthy: `repadmin /replsummary` should show no
  failures. A rotation that does not reach every DC causes Kerberos failures.
- Read-only DCs have their own krbtgt_XXXXX accounts. Microsoft's script can handle those too.
- Rotate **twice**, with a wait between the rotations. The first change invalidates nothing on
  its own (the old key is still accepted as the previous key). The second change invalidates
  every ticket signed with the original key. Rotating twice in quick succession can break
  existing sessions and services before their tickets renew.
- Schedule the work in a change window and tell the service desk. Users may need to log off and on.

## Fix
### Option A: Microsoft's New-KrbtgtKeys.ps1 (recommended)
1. Download `New-KrbtgtKeys.ps1` from Microsoft's official GitHub repository (see References).
2. Run it on a domain-joined admin host as a Domain Admin. Start with the **simulation** /
   read-only test modes it offers to check that all DCs are reachable and replicating.
3. Run the **reset** mode for the domain's krbtgt account (first rotation).
4. Wait at least the maximum user ticket lifetime (10 hours by default, see
   **Default Domain Policy > Kerberos Policy**) **and** until replication of the change to every
   DC is confirmed. Many organisations wait 24 hours.
5. Run the reset mode a second time (second rotation).
6. Repeat the double rotation at least every 180 days. After a suspected compromise, do it
   immediately.

### Option B: Manual reset
In **Active Directory Users and Computers**, enable **View > Advanced Features**, right-click
**krbtgt** in the Users container > **Reset Password** and enter any value. Windows replaces it
with a random password. Repeat after the wait described above. The script is preferred because
it verifies replication.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Check the current password age
Get-ADUser -Identity krbtgt -Properties PasswordLastSet | Select-Object Name, PasswordLastSet

# Confirm replication health before and between rotations
repadmin /replsummary

# Run Microsoft's script and follow its menu: simulation first, then reset.
# Run it twice in total, waiting >= max ticket lifetime (default 10h) and for full
# replication between the two resets.
.\New-KrbtgtKeys.ps1
```

## Verify
`Get-ADUser krbtgt -Properties PasswordLastSet` shows a recent date, and `repadmin /showobjmeta
<DC> "CN=krbtgt,CN=Users,DC=<domain>,DC=<tld>"` shows the same unicodePwd version on every DC.
Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

## Rollback
A krbtgt rotation cannot be undone. If clients report Kerberos errors after the first rotation,
wait for replication to finish and have affected users log off and on (or run `klist purge`).
Do not perform the second rotation until the first has fully replicated.

## References
- https://github.com/microsoft/New-KrbtgtKeys.ps1
- https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1558/001/
- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/ad-forest-recovery-resetting-the-krbtgt-password
guides.PW-023:
# PW-023: Non-Tier Zero principal can log on to domain controllers

**Category:** Hygiene
**Typical owner:** AD / identity team

## What this finding means
A user, computer or group outside Tier Zero can open a session on domain
controllers through Remote Desktop, PowerShell remoting (WinRM) or DCOM. On a
domain controller these rights do not come from a local group, because DCs have
no local accounts database. They come from the domain's built-in groups:
**Remote Desktop Users** (S-1-5-32-555), **Remote Management Users**
(S-1-5-32-580) and **Distributed COM Users** (S-1-5-32-562). These groups are
shared by every DC in the domain. A GPO linked to the Domain Controllers OU can
also grant them.

Pathwarden does not draw this as an attack path: a session alone is not control
of the domain. It is one step from it, though.

## Why attackers care
A logon on a DC puts an attacker's code on the most sensitive server in the
domain. One local privilege escalation (an unpatched driver, a misconfigured
service, a token impersonation bug) turns it into SYSTEM on the DC, which means
the NTDS.dit database, every password hash and the krbtgt key (OS Credential
Dumping: NTDS, T1003.003). It also lets the attacker read whatever the DC
exposes to logged-on users: scripts, shares and memory left by other sessions.

## Before you change anything
- Find out who uses the access and why. Helpdesk and monitoring teams are
  often given RDP to DCs "temporarily", and some monitoring agents use WinRM.
- Monitoring and management tools that need WinRM on DCs should use a
  dedicated, tightly scoped account, ideally in Tier Zero and managed as such,
  or a pull model that needs no inbound logon.
- Check whether the right comes from group membership (most common) or from a
  GPO user right on the Domain Controllers OU; the finding's fix lists both.

## Fix
### Option A: Empty the built-in groups (recommended)
1. In **Active Directory Users and Computers**, open the **Builtin** container
   of the domain.
2. Open **Remote Desktop Users**, **Remote Management Users** and
   **Distributed COM Users**, and remove the principal from the finding (and
   anything else that is not Tier Zero).
3. Leave Domain Admins and other Tier Zero administrators as they are: they
   can already log on to DCs through Administrators.
### Option B: Remove GPO-granted logon rights
1. In **Group Policy Management**, review every GPO linked to the **Domain
   Controllers** OU (usually only the Default Domain Controllers Policy).
2. Under **Computer Configuration > Policies > Windows Settings > Security
   Settings > Local Policies > User Rights Assignment**, check **Allow log on
   through Remote Desktop Services** and **Access this computer from the
   network**, and remove the principal from both.

### PowerShell
```powershell
Import-Module ActiveDirectory

# Who is in the built-in remote access groups?
'Remote Desktop Users', 'Remote Management Users', 'Distributed COM Users' |
    ForEach-Object { Get-ADGroupMember -Identity $_ -Recursive | Select-Object @{ n = 'Group'; e = { $_ } }, Name, objectClass }

# Remove the principal from the finding
Remove-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Remote Desktop Users' -Members '<Principal>' -Confirm:$false
```

## Verify
A Remote Desktop or `Enter-PSSession` attempt by the principal to a listed DC
must be refused. Collect again (or use Retest in the app, or `pathwarden retest` on the CLI) and confirm the finding ID is gone.

## Rollback
Add the principal back with
`Add-ADGroupMember -Identity '<Group>' -Members '<Principal>'`, or restore the
user right in the GPO and run `gpupdate /force` on the domain controllers.
